paragraphs.heading: A kingdom of their own
paragraphs.text: A fungus is a eukaryotic organism, a living thing whose cells hold membrane-bound nuclei, and the group includes yeasts, molds and mushrooms. Biologists place all of them in a separate kingdom called Fungi. One trait that sets fungi apart from plants and bacteria is chitin in their cell walls. A fungus does not carry out photosynthesis.

paragraphs.heading: How fungi feed and move
paragraphs.text: Like animals, fungi are heterotrophs: they need ready-made organic compounds for energy. A fungus usually releases digestive enzymes into its surroundings and then soaks up the dissolved food molecules. It does not walk or swim; it gets around by growing, though its spores can drift through air or water. Most fungi go unnoticed because their parts are tiny and they live hidden in soil or on dead matter. They catch the eye mainly when they fruit, as mushrooms or as molds.

paragraphs.heading: Closer to animals than plants
paragraphs.text: The true fungi form one related group that shares a common ancestor, a view strongly backed by molecular studies of their family tree. They are kept apart from look-alikes such as slime molds and water molds. The study of fungi is called mycology, from a Greek word for mushroom. It was once treated as a branch of botany, but fungi are now known to be genetically closer to animals than to plants.

paragraphs.heading: Recyclers and partners
paragraphs.text: Fungi are the main decomposers in nature, breaking down dead organic matter and keeping nutrients moving through the environment. Fungi include partners of plants, animals and other fungi, as well as parasites. More than 90% of plants depend on a partnership with fungi known as mycorrhizal symbiosis. That partnership also boosts the capture of carbon from the air, which helps ease climate change.

paragraphs.heading: Useful to people
paragraphs.text: People have long eaten fungi in the form of mushrooms and truffles. Fungi also make bread rise and ferment foods and drinks such as wine, beer and soy sauce. Since the 1940s they have been used to make antibiotics, and enzymes from fungi now go into industry and detergents. Some are even put to work as living pesticides against weeds, plant diseases and insect pests.

paragraphs.heading: The harmful side
paragraphs.text: Many species make poisons called mycotoxins that harm animals, people included. Fungi can wear down buildings and manufactured materials, and some cause serious disease in humans and other animals. Fungal crop diseases such as rice blast, along with food spoilage, can hurt food supplies and local economies. More than 8,000 species are known to harm plants, and at least 300 can cause disease in humans.

paragraphs.heading: A kingdom barely mapped
paragraphs.text: The fungus kingdom stretches from single-celled chytrids living in water to large mushrooms. Estimates put the total at 2.2 million to 3.8 million species, yet only about 148,000 have been described. For centuries fungi were sorted by their form, such as spore color, or by how they work. DNA studies in the first ten years of this century reshaped that scheme into one subkingdom, seven phyla and ten subphyla.
